name: Docmost
tagline: Open source collaborative wiki and docs workspace, a self-hostable Confluence/Notion alternative.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A personal wiki is one of the most one-shottable things in software: a page tree, a rich text editor, full text search, and a SQLite file will cover most of what one person actually does in Docmost. The gaps start where other humans do, specifically real time collaborative editing, comments, spaces with permissions, and invite flows, all of which are genuinely annoying to build and genuinely load-bearing for a team. There is also an awkward fact here: Docmost is already open source and self-hostable for free, so a DIY build is competing with a free product that someone else maintains. If you want a private notes brain, build it in a weekend and enjoy owning the schema. If you want a wiki your coworkers will actually write in, run Docmost itself or pay for the cloud and stop reinventing the editor.
coreLoopDIY: A local-first wiki: nested pages with a rich text editor, instant full text search, backlinks, and markdown import/export, all in one SQLite file.
requirements: A place to run it: laptop, NAS, or a small VPS
Optional S3-compatible bucket or local disk for file uploads
whatYouLose: Real time multiplayer editing with cursors, which is a Yjs/CRDT project of its own
Comments, mentions, and page level discussion
Spaces, groups, and granular permissions for anyone who is not you
Hosted backups, upgrades, and SSO/SAML if you ever grow past one person
Mobile-friendly polish and the hundred small editor behaviors that only show up after a year of users
moatNotes: The moat is other people being in the document with you. For an audience of one, that moat is a puddle.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because the self-hosted version is free but running it is not: upgrades, Postgres, Redis, object storage, TLS, and backups add up to a chore nobody volunteers for. The cloud tier buys away that chore plus SSO and support, which is exactly the line where a company stops caring whether the software is open source. For individuals the calculus is different, which is why the single-user case is the one worth building yourself.
notes: The editor is the whole product, so spend your time there and ignore everything else.
prompt:
Build a single-user, self-hosted wiki app called "Pages" in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions:
- TypeScript everywhere.
- Backend: Node 20 + Hono, SQLite via better-sqlite3. No ORM, hand-written SQL and a migrations folder.
- Frontend: Vite + React + Tailwind, TipTap for the editor.
- One process serves the API and the built frontend.

Data model:
- pages(id, parent_id nullable, title, content_json, content_text, position, created_at, updated_at, archived_at nullable)
- attachments(id, page_id, filename, mime, size, path)
- SQLite FTS5 virtual table over title + content_text, kept in sync with triggers.

Features that are in scope:
- Sidebar page tree with unlimited nesting, drag to reorder and reparent, collapse state persisted in localStorage.
- TipTap editor: headings, bold/italic/strike/code, bullet and ordered lists, task lists, blockquote, code blocks with highlight.js, tables, horizontal rule, images, links.
- Slash menu for block insertion and a markdown-style input rules setup (typing "# " makes a heading).
- Autosave with a 600ms debounce, PATCH to the API, show a small "saved" indicator. No save button.
- Full text search in a cmd+K palette, FTS5 with snippet() highlighting, results jump to the page.
- [[wiki links]]: autocomplete page titles while typing, store as a TipTap mark with a page id, render a "Linked from" backlinks list at the bottom of each page.
- Attachment upload to ./data/uploads, served from the API, inline for images.
- Import: drop a folder of .md files and create pages mirroring the directory structure. Export: download the whole wiki as a zip of markdown files.
- Archive instead of delete, with a trash view and restore.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build:
- Accounts, signup, user tables, roles, permissions.
- Real time collaboration, comments, mentions, notifications.
- Telemetry, analytics, any outbound network call.

Auth: a single shared password from PASSWORD in .env, checked once, set an httpOnly signed cookie. Ship .env.example only. If PASSWORD is unset, run open on localhost and print a warning.

Ops: everything lives in ./data (pages.db, uploads). Add an npm script that copies ./data to a timestamped backup folder. Write a Dockerfile and a docker-compose.yml with ./data mounted as a volume.

Deliver a README with setup, backup, and a short note on how to restore. Seed the database with three example pages on first run so the tree is not empty.
